idiom_name: HashMap<Long, List<Entity>> keyed by packed cell coordinates
implementation_notes: The JDK has no spatial index; the manual realization is a HashMap<Long, List<Entity>> keyed by a packed cell coordinate (two 32-bit ints packed into one long) with computeIfAbsent as the insert idiom, or a List<Entity>[][] array grid for bounded worlds. HashMap is unsynchronized and relies on hashCode/equals, so packed primitive keys or immutable records are preferred over mutable key objects. The hash grid is the default for dynamic entity worlds; JTS STRtree is the alternative when the workload is geometry-shaped over mostly static data.
pitfalls: HashMap is not synchronized; a game loop and an AI or network thread mutating the grid need confinement or a concurrent map.
Packing two ints into a long must sign-extend carefully; the obvious (cx << 32) | cy collides for negative cy unless masked.
Removing entities from the middle of a List is linear; swap-and-pop or a per-cell Set keeps removal cheap.

variants.name: JTS STRtree (packed R-tree)
variants.implementation_notes: JTS ships STRtree, a Sort-Tile-Recursive packed R-tree: insert(Envelope, Object), query(Envelope), remove and nearest-neighbour queries with an ItemDistance (locationtech JTS javadoc). It is semi-static - the tree is built on first query and items can no longer be added afterwards - so it replaces the classic grid only for build-once or batch workloads; constantly moving entities keep the hash-grid realization. Querying is thread-safe once built, insertion is not.
pitfalls: After the first query the tree cannot take new items, so a dynamic world must rebuild it instead of updating incrementally.
Results are Object and need a cast (as in the sketch), and query returns items whose envelopes intersect, not exact hits.
Nearest-neighbour queries need an ItemDistance implementation; the default only compares envelopes.
